query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A single, controlled pre‐oxidation treatment performed at an intermediate temperature (1000°C) in a low‐oxygen atmosphere for 10 hours will form a thin, uniform, and adherent protective oxide scale that significantly improves the high‐temperature oxygen resistance of a refractory high‐entropy alloy during subsequent exposure at 1100°C in an air environment for 100 hours.
generation.material_initial_state: Untreated refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., a MoNbTaTiW‐based RHEA) that, when exposed to high temperatures in oxygen‐rich environments, naturally forms rapidly growing and non‐protective oxide scales.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to a controlled pre‐oxidation treatment by heating at approximately 1000°C for 10 hours in a low‐oxygen (or oxygen‐diluted) atmosphere to form a tailored protective surface oxide layer.
generation.conditions: Pre‐oxidation: 1000°C for 10 hours in a controlled, low‐oxygen atmosphere; Service exposure: 1100°C in an air (oxygen‐rich) environment for 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, uniform, self‐healing oxide scale (preferably enriched in protective oxides such as Al2O3 or SiO2) that acts as an effective diffusion barrier against oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: The pre‐oxidation treatment promotes the early formation of a stable, compact oxide layer that adheres strongly to the alloy surface. This engineered layer limits further oxygen diffusion during high‐temperature exposure, suppressing the formation and spallation of non‐protective oxide scales that normally degrade the material.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to an untreated RHEA, the pre‐oxidized alloy is expected to show a significantly lower mass gain (indicative of slower oxidation kinetics) and enhanced oxide scale integrity, maintaining structural stability during extended exposure at 1100°C in air.
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory high‐entropy alloys typically develop rapidly growing, non‐protective oxide scales that experience spallation and exhibit high mass gain under extreme high‐temperature oxidation conditions.
generation.boundary: This improvement is anticipated for service conditions at 1100°C in an air (or oxygen‐rich) environment for durations around 100 hours. The effect may vary with the specific alloy composition and the precise conditions of the pre‐oxidation treatment.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the uniformity and composition of the pre‐formed oxide layer, which may depend on slight variations in alloy composition and the exact oxygen partial pressure during treatment. The extent of improvement in oxidation resistance might also vary with small deviations in processing temperatures and times.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical MoNbTaTiW-based RHEA samples. Subject one set to the controlled pre‐oxidation treatment (heating at 1000°C for 10 hours in a low‐oxygen atmosphere) while leaving the other set untreated. Then, expose both sets to an air environment at 1100°C for 100 hours. Post-treatment, perform a comparative analysis using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and microstructural characterization.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area (mg/cm²) measured over time during the 1100°C exposure
Oxide scale thickness, uniformity, and adherence assessed via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and cross-sectional imaging
Phase composition and identification of protective oxides (e.g., Al2O3 or SiO2) using X-ray diffraction (XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre‐oxidized samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in mass gain and improvement in oxide scale integrity (i.e., formation of a continuous, adherent, and protective oxide layer) compared to the untreated samples during the 1100°C exposure, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. frame.system: Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEAs) intended for structural applications at extreme temperatures, currently in their untreated state with insufficient high‐temperature oxidation resistance.
frame.goal: Improve the high‐temperature oxygen resistance so that the alloy maintains its structural integrity over extended exposure in oxygen‐rich, extreme-temperature environments.
frame.limitation: The untreated alloy forms non‐protective, rapidly growing oxide scales at high temperatures, leading to degradation under oxygen exposure.
constraints: single intervention must be applied (i.e., only one change to the alloy system)
the intervention must yield a clear, measurable improvement relative to the untreated alloy
the hypothesis must define specific temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions
must be relevant for structural applications in extreme environments
frame.regime: For example, an operating condition of approximately 1100°C in an air (or oxygen‐rich) atmosphere for extended durations (e.g., 100 hours) is anticipated, simulating extreme service conditions for high-temperature applications.
prior_attempts: Conventional RHEA formulations and multi-component coatings have been attempted but either did not form stable, adherent oxide scales or required complex multi-step processing that is impractical for structural alloys.

decision.trend: Early oxidation studies (e.g., PMC6317005) characterized the uncontrolled, rapidly growing oxidized scales on untreated refractory HEAs at high temperatures, noting a switch from parabolic to breakaway kinetics that undermine long‐term stability. Later work (e.g., PMC7475834) demonstrated that applying multi‐component silicide coatings (Si–Cr–Fe based) can tailor the surface reactions to form more complex, layered oxide structures. However, although these coatings can improve oxidation resistance, they require complex processing and yield non‐ideal multi‐layered structures unsuited to structural applications.
decision.unsolved: The key unresolved issue is finding a single, simple intervention that can convert the unstable, fast-growing oxidized scale of an untreated RHEA into a thin, self-healing, and protective barrier at extreme temperatures without altering the bulk alloy composition or requiring multi‐step processing.
decision.lever: A controlled pre‐oxidation treatment that intentionally forms a uniform and adherent protective oxide scale (for example, an Al2O3‐ or SiO2‐rich layer) on the alloy surface. This would involve exposing the untreated alloy at an intermediate temperature (~1000°C) in a controlled, low‐oxygen (or oxygen‐diluted) atmosphere for a defined period (e.g., 10 hours) so that the surface oxidizes in a controlled manner prior to service at 1100°C in air for 100 hours.
decision.why: Building on the insights from earlier studies, this approach targets the oxidation weakness directly by engineering the alloy surface. Similar in spirit to the beneficial effects seen with silicide coatings but far simpler, the pre‐oxidation treatment aims to create a stable, self‐limiting oxide layer that impedes further oxygen ingress during extreme service. This single-step surface modification directly addresses the gap in achieving a practical, scalable improvement in high-temperature oxygen resistance while avoiding the complexities of multi-component coatings.
